steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computer vision paper on learning degradation-independent representations (DiR) of images produced by camera ISP pipelines. Explain why ISP degradations are hard to model, introduce our self-supervised DiRNet and its refinement branch, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Digital cameras everywhere; human-vision vs. machine-vision applications
- Different image quality needs for the two
- ISP pipeline and signal-level degradations
- ISP hyperparameters as a second, semantic-level degradation
- Our idea: degradation-independent representation (DiR), DiRNet
- Refinement with an auxiliary branch and alignment module
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Cameras
  - information era: digital cameras ubiquitous, indispensable in socioeconomic life
  - most common sensory device for humans and their intelligent agents
  - two categories by end purpose: human vision oriented (smartphones, social media, internet videos) vs. machine vision oriented (robotics, automation, medical imaging)
- Quality requirements
  - human vision: metrics should match human visual perception, images meant to please our eyes
  - machine vision: requirements may not align with human perception; what matters = preserving semantically critical features for recognition / classification
- ISP pipeline (same acquisition either way)
  - hardware ISP: raw Bayer sensor data -> RGB
  - cascaded steps: denoising, color demosaicking, compression; each can degrade quality
  - sensor noise (esp. dark, low SNR) -> demosaicking adds interpolation noise -> compression for bandwidth adds compression noise
  - compound effects very hard to model precisely
  - so cannot synthesize clean/degraded pairs for supervised learning
- Second type: ISP hyperparameters
  - gamma correction, ISO, gain control, white balance
  - optimal settings vary per application, no one-fits-all
  - defaults tailored to perceptual quality, not to a specific CV task
  - deviations from optimal settings = degradations too
  - can cause underperformance or failure of downstream CV algorithms
  - semantic-level, extremely hard to model/synthesize: very high-dim hyperparameter space; two types intertwined
- DiR
  - degraded / degradation-free (ground truth) pairs intractable or very expensive
  - can't exhaust all degradation variants; many not known or understood
  - DiR: robust to camera-captured non-ideal real-world images; new deep network approach to learn it
  - Fig. 1: DiR paradigm vs. canonical paradigm
  - DiR holds intrinsic info of the degradation-free image -> more general/robust to unseen degradation types and severity in downstream tasks
  - DiRNet, self-supervised; two objectives: any two degraded images -> same DiR; all DiRs sampled from normal distribution -> VAE by multi-view mutual information (MMI) maximization
- Refinement
  - use known ISP priors to synthesize original/degraded pairs -> auxiliary self-supervised branch
  - branch learns reference representation \mathbf{r}^{\ast} of degradation-free images from high-quality images (surrogate ground truth)
  - alignment module: baseline DiR \mathbf{r}^{(0)} aligned statistically to \mathbf{r}^{\ast} (DfR), trained on synthesized pairs -> refined DiR \mathbf{r}^{+} for downstream tasks
  - best of self-supervised and supervised; balance robustness vs. precision
- Contributions
  - self-supervised DiR learning by multivariate mutual information maximization, only degraded training images
  - joint learning to refine DiR for the targeted end-task network
  - versatility across image restoration, object detection, instance segmentation; ample empirical evidence

They are probably the most common type of sensory device that both humans and their intelligent agents use to sense the environment. Applications of digital imaging can be split into two categories based on what they are used for in the end: human vision oriented and machine vision oriented. Smartphones, social media, internet videos, etc. are examples of the first category, and robotics, automation, and medical imaging are examples of the second one.

For human vision oriented applications, the image quality metrics should match human visual perception, since the images are mainly meant to please our eyes. steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In our information era, digital cameras are everywhere and they are indispensable in all parts of socioeconomic life. They are probably the most common type of sensory device that both humans and their intelligent agents use to sense the environment. Applications of digital imaging can be split into two categories based on what they are used for in the end: human vision oriented and machine vision oriented. Smartphones, social media, internet videos, etc. are examples of the first category, and robotics, automation, and medical imaging are examples of the second one.

For human vision oriented applications, the image quality metrics should match human visual perception, since the images are mainly meant to please our eyes. For machine vision oriented applications, on the other hand, the image quality requirements may not fully match those of human perception. In this case what matters most is keeping the semantically critical image features that are needed for solving computer vision problems of recognition and classification nature.

Whether the images are for human viewing or for downstream computer vision tasks, the image acquisition process of digital cameras is the same. All images are generated by a hardware image signal processing (ISP) pipeline which turns raw Bayer sensor data into RGB images. The ISP pipeline is a set of cascaded steps, including denoising, color demosaicking, and compression. Each of these steps can degrade the image quality to some level. At the start of the ISP pipeline there are sensor noises, especially in dark environments where the signal-to-noise ratio is low. The noisy RAW data are then demosaiced to get the RGB images. This demosaicking process introduces its own interpolation noises. Last, the RGB image is compressed for bandwidth efficiency, which adds compression noises on top of the sensor noises and demosaicking noises. The compound effects of all these cascaded noises are very difficult to model precisely. Because the image quality degradation mechanism underneath is so complex, we cannot synthesize clean and degraded image pairs for supervised learning.

There is also another type of ISP degradation that has bad effects when ISP-generated images are used in downstream tasks. The camera ISP has a number of adjustable hyperparameters such as gamma correction, ISO, gain control, and white balance. Their optimal settings can be different from application to application, so there is no one-fits-all solution. Most cameras have a default hyperparameter setting that is tailored to perceptual quality and not optimized for a specific computer vision task. In a general sense, we consider deviations of ISP hyperparameters from their optimal settings to be degradations too. This second type of ISP degradation can make downstream computer vision algorithms underperform or even fail outright. Like the first type of signal-level degradations, this second type of semantic-level degradations is extremely difficult, if not impossible, to model and synthesize. One reason is that the space of ISP hyperparameters is very high-dimensional, and another is that the two types of ISP degradations are intertwined.

So, as discussed above, getting pairs of ISP-degraded images and the corresponding latent degradation-free (ground truth) images is either intractable or very expensive. Also, it is impossible to exhaust all ISP degradation variants by brute force, and many of them are not even known or understood. To deal with these challenges, we introduce the notion of a degradation-independent latent representation (DiR) which is robust against camera-captured non-ideal real-world images, and we propose a new deep neural network approach to learn the DiR. Fig. 1 shows the difference between our DiR learning paradigm and the canonical learning paradigm. In our DiR learning framework, the learned DiR representations contain intrinsic information of the original degradation-free image, so it is more general and robust to unseen degradation types and severity when it is used in downstream computer vision and image processing tasks. The DiR learning is done by a deep neural network called DiRNet and is self-supervised. The DiRNet is trained with two learning objectives: any two degraded images are mapped to the same DiR, and all DiRs are sampled from a normal distribution. This is learning a variational auto-encoder (VAE) by multi-view mutual information (MMI) maximization.

In addition, we use known priors of the ISP workflow to synthesize original and degraded pairs, so that the baseline DiR above can be reinforced by an auxiliary self-supervised learning branch. This auxiliary branch learns the reference representation \mathbf{r}^{\ast} of the degradation-free images, using high-quality images (surrogate ground truth). An alignment network module statistically aligns the baseline DiR result \mathbf{r}^{(0)} with the result \mathbf{r}^{\ast} of the auxiliary branch. The alignment module is trained with the synthesized pairs mentioned above and it learns to align the baseline DiR \mathbf{r}^{(0)} to the degradation-free representation reference (DfR) \mathbf{r}^{\ast}, which gives a refined DiR \mathbf{r}^{+}. In the end, the refined DiR \mathbf{r}^{+} is ready to be used in downstream tasks. Overall, the refined DiR gets the best of both self-supervised and supervised learning, and it strikes a good balance between robustness and precision of the model for applications.

Our main contributions and key results are:

- We propose a new method for self-supervised learning of the DiR representation by multivariate mutual information maximization, which only needs degraded training images.

- We use a joint learning approach to refine the DiR representation so that it performs optimally in the targeted end-task network.

- We give ample empirical evidence that the proposed methods are versatile across a wide range of tasks, including image restoration, object detection, and instance segmentation.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In our information era, digital cameras have become ubiquitous and indispensable in all walks of socioeconomic life. They are arguably the most common type of sensory device for both humans and their intelligent agents to sense the environment. Depending on their end purposes, the applications of digital imaging fall into two categories: human vision oriented and machine vision oriented. Examples of the first category include smartphones, social media, internet videos, etc., whereas robotics, automation, and medical imaging belong to the second category.

For human vision oriented applications, the image quality metrics should correspond to human visual perception, because the images are primarily intended to please our eyes. For machine vision oriented applications [1,2,3,4], on the other hand, the image quality requirements may not completely align with those of human perception. In the latter case, what matters most is preserving the semantically critical image features that are needed to solve computer vision problems of recognition and classification nature.

For either human viewing or downstream computer vision tasks, the image acquisition process of digital cameras is the same. All images are generated by a hardware image signal processing (ISP) pipeline that transforms raw Bayer sensor data into RGB images. The ISP pipeline consists of a set of cascaded steps, including denoising, color demosaicking, and compression, each of which can cause some degradation in image quality. At the beginning of the ISP pipeline, there are sensor noises, particularly in dark environments with a low signal-to-noise ratio. The noisy RAW data are then demosaiced to produce the corresponding RGB images, and this demosaicking process introduces interpolation noises of its own. Finally, the RGB image is compressed for bandwidth efficiency, adding extra compression noises on top of sensor noises and demosaicking noises. The resulting compound effects of these cascaded noises are very difficult to model precisely [5]. This complex underlying degradation mechanism prevents the synthesis of clean and degraded image pairs for supervised learning.

Yet there is another type of ISP degradation that has adverse effects on the use of ISP-generated images in downstream tasks. The camera ISP involves a number of adjustable hyperparameters such as gamma correction, ISO, gain control, and white balance. Their optimal settings may vary from application to application; there is no one-fits-all solution. Most cameras have a default hyperparameter setting that is tailored to perceptual quality rather than optimized for a specific computer vision task. In a general sense, we consider the deviations of ISP hyperparameters from their optimal settings to be degradations as well. This second type of ISP degradation can lead to underperformance or even outright failure of downstream computer vision algorithms [6,7]. Like the first type of signal-level degradations, the second type of semantic-level degradations is extremely difficult, if not impossible, to model and synthesize, both because the space of ISP hyperparameters is very high-dimensional and because the two types of ISP degradations are intertwined.

As discussed above, it is either intractable or highly expensive to obtain pairs of ISP-degraded and corresponding latent degradation-free (ground truth) images. Moreover, it is impossible to exhaust all ISP degradation variants by brute force, many of which are not even known or understood [8,9]. To meet these challenges, we introduce the notion of a degradation-independent latent representation (DiR) that is robust against camera-captured non-ideal real-world images, and propose a new deep neural network approach to learn the DiR. Fig. 1 illustrates the difference between our DiR learning paradigm and the canonical learning paradigm. Within our DiR learning framework, the learned DiR representations contain intrinsic information of the original degradation-free image, and hence are more general and robust to unseen degradation types and severity when used in downstream computer vision and image processing tasks. The DiR learning, carried out by a deep neural network called DiRNet, is self-supervised, and the DiRNet is trained with two learning objectives: any two degraded images are mapped to the same DiR, and all DiRs are sampled from a normal distribution, which amounts to learning a variational auto-encoder (VAE) by multi-view mutual information (MMI) maximization [10,11,12].

Moreover, we exploit known priors of the ISP workflow to synthesize original and degraded pairs, so that the baseline DiR above can be reinforced by an auxiliary self-supervised learning branch. This auxiliary branch learns the reference representation \mathbf{r}^{\ast} of the degradation-free images, using high-quality images (surrogate ground truth). An alignment network module statistically aligns the baseline DiR result \mathbf{r}^{(0)} with the result \mathbf{r}^{\ast} of the auxiliary branch. Trained on the aforementioned synthesized pairs, this alignment module learns to align the baseline DiR \mathbf{r}^{(0)} to the degradation-free representation reference (DfR) \mathbf{r}^{\ast}, yielding a refined DiR \mathbf{r}^{+}, which is then ready for use in downstream tasks. Overall, the refined DiR benefits from the best of both self-supervised and supervised learning, and strikes a good balance between the model's robustness and precision for applications.

Our main contributions and key results can be summarized as follows:

- We propose a novel method for self-supervised learning of the DiR representation by multivariate mutual information maximization, which requires only degraded training images.

- We employ a joint learning approach to refine the DiR representation for optimal performance in the targeted end-task network.

- We provide ample empirical evidence for the versatility of the proposed methods across a wide range of tasks, including image restoration, object detection, and instance segmentation.
